panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: H&E histology of the resected hemangioma from a Maffucci syndrome patient showing large cavernous blood-filled vascular spaces, the hallmark vascular lesion of Maffucci syndrome. Caption and in-text explicitly attribute this panel to the Maffucci syndrome case. B: H&E histology showing the spindle cell hemangioma component of the same Maffucci syndrome patient's lesion. Spindle cell hemangioma is a recognized but less common histological component in Maffucci syndrome hemangiomas. No direct vocabulary key exists for this finding; captured as proposed finding. C: H&E histology at higher magnification showing sheets of vacuolated cells (vacuolated endothelial cells) within the same Maffucci syndrome hemangioma. This is a recognized histological feature described in the in-text. No direct vocabulary key exists; captured as proposed finding.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (a, b, c, d). a: Axial chest CT of a patient with Maffucci syndrome showing a destructive lytic (chondromatous/enchondroma) lesion of the rib and sternum consistent with multiple enchondromas with cortical breach. b: Second axial chest CT of the same patient showing the destructive lytic chondromatous lesion, part of Maffucci syndrome enchondromatosis. c: Sagittal chest CT of the same Maffucci syndrome patient demonstrating the large destructive sternal lesion attributable to enchondromatosis. d: Frontal (coronal) chest CT of the same Maffucci syndrome patient showing multiple chondromatous/lytic lesions of the chest wall and sternum.

in_text_mentions: The CT scan of the chest revealed a large, well-circumscribed, destructive lytic lesion (11.7 × 13.1 × 11.2 mm) that had extended into the left lung and mediastinum, confirmed as chondroma by histological analysis. Additionally, a CT scan demonstrates numerous lesions on the sternum, left 5, 6, and 7 ribs, scapula, and humerus (on both sides) with a maximal size of 60 × 49 × 44 mm. There are numerous nodular lesions with calcifications on the anterior chest wall, the largest of which can measure up to 2.3 × 1.0 cm (Figure 3).
